utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, continue your examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Welcome back, Officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, before going on, I noted yesterday that I did not tender ter number 129. That's the collection of photographs that we spent some time on yesterday. I tender that at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P264, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And then if I could please ask the court officer to call up the chart that we ended the day on yesterday, which is ter number 145B.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Officer, do you see this chart once again on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Yesterday, we noted that there were some dimensions on this chart. Can you tell us, who took those measurements, and how; what tools they used; how they made sure the measurements were accurate.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A colleague of mine, Salko Cerimagic, prepared this sketch because it's impossible for person to do that due to the sizes. So the two of us did it together and did these measurements.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Is there a measurement there from the impact crater to the curb?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And how far is it from the centre of the impact crater, which I believe is the circled 1, to the curb?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's about 1.90 metres or 1.85 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And is there also a dimension noted from the curb to the wall of the building up against which those two bicycles were leaning?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're not written here, but the distance is either 2.90 or 2.60.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. And so a summing up of those dimensions would give us the distance from the centre of the impact crater to the wall of the building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When you add them up, it's either 4.60 or 4.50.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you. And at this time, Your Honour, also I will tender the large photo montage, which is up behind the witness, for Your Honours to consult later if a very detailed photograph is thought useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P265, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Officer, did you write a report concerning your work at Markale market on the 28th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We made the markings and prepared a short forensic report giving a short description and the number of casualties or the dead people who were processed in the morgue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: If we could please see 65 ter number 145B, e-court page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for that to come up, Officer, were efforts made to identify those who had died at the scene?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, you mean the dead persons? Though it wasn't impossible to do it on the spot, but lots of papers were found on the location which we photographed, and later on they were used for identification in the Kosevo Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Among the photographs that we put into evidence, are there photographs of these identity documents, handbags, wallets, and so forth that were found at Markale market?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a lot of identification papers and personal belongings were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: On the page that is on the monitor in front of you, there is a list of 35 names. Do you see that list of names?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: What names are these? Whose names are these?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The names of the citizens who died as a result of this projectile, and they were identified at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Is this is a complete list of all of those who eventually died from this projectile?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Approximately another 30 persons succumbed to the injuries that they had received.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And so in addition to these 35, there are some additional names; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I have no further questions in direct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, and thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, I am a Defence counsel of the accused General Milosevic, and I would kindly ask you to give me answers to certain questions that you already answered in response to the Prosecutor's question and, if possible, to give me as brief answers as possible in order for us to wrap up this cross-examination as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness first be shown document 65 ter 1484, tendered by the Defence under number D19.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let's first look at -- can you see page 1 and what is written here: "Sarajevo, 18 November 1994. With a single sniper shot fired at around 1300 hours from the aggressor positions from the Metalka building at Grbavica at the intersection of Zmaja od Bosne and Franje Rackog Streets, a boy, Nermin Divovic, born in 1987, was fatally wounded in the head, and his mother, Dzenana Sokolovic, received a serious wound to the stomach." My question is: You took part in the investigation relating to this incident?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I assisted my colleague who was this charge, and given the circumstances where it happened, the two of us were sent out to do the on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now look at page 3. Yes, page 3. Page 3, description of the event, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read it out to you. In order for me not to read everything, I will begin where it says: "Nermin Divovic, a boy born in 1987, was fatally wounded while his mother Dzenana Sokolovic," born on that and that year, "was seriously wounded. The bullet passed through the boy's head and then seriously wounded his mother in the stomach." Is that what you established on the scene?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was impossible to establish that on the scene because the casualties were not there. We only came afterwards in order to carry out the on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Tapuskovic please turn off his microphone while the witness is speaking; otherwise, there's overlapping.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... established in this description --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The interpreter has asked, Mr. Tapuskovic, that you turn off the microphone while the witness is speaking; otherwise, there is overlapping. And the witness is also protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, this report is not correct; right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report was made by an operative on the scene who collected information from the people present on the spot. I didn't write this report; neither did my colleague who carried out the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you did gather all physical evidence relating to this incident, and what is written here was prepared based on the evidence, among other things, based on medical record as well?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the two of us didn't do it. Our task was to photograph the scene, make a sketch thereof on the basis of the clues and the traces that we found. That's our description. However, taking statements from witnesses was not our duty. This refers to the processing of the scene by a forensic technician. This applies to medical reports as well. This is done by a forensic expert who prepares official reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So this medical record served as a basis for your establishing the facts?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In any case that's true, but this document is part of the whole process and the procedure, and then later on it's forwarded to the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can I please draw your attention to page 15 of this same 65 ter document. Page 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. The witness has disavowed knowledge of this report, has said that he did not prepare this report, has said that his colleague did not prepare this report, and while I have no objection to the witness being questioned about this incident, I do have an objection to him being questioned on the basis of this report which he has said he knows nothing of more than once in response to counsel's questions. So my objection is lack of foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll hear the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we just for a moment go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you worked on collecting physical evidence; right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thereafter, the prosecutor's office in charge received everything that you had gathered.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at page 15 of this document, please. That's a criminal report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you can see this criminal report sent to the prosecutor's office. It's dated the 14th of December. So after a good two months and after everything you did, according to the laws applicable in Bosnia-Herzegovina, your team submitted -- filed a criminal report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I wasn't involved in preparing this criminal report so I know nothing about the date. Our exclusive duty was to prepare a photo file, to make a sketch of the scene and the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It's only reasonable because it's within the competence of the high prosecutor's office. But look at what it says here. It's a criminal report against an unknown perpetrator. Look at the middle of the passage of the statement of reasons. Let us begin with "Sarajevo" -- no, let's start with "On this occasion ..." Can you see that? Can you see it? "On this occasion, the bullet passed through the head of the child Nermin Divovic, born 1987 in Sarajevo, and then seriously wounded his mother Dzenana Sokolovic to the stomach." Did the public prosecutor, based on your documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not speak B/C/S, but at least in the English translation on the left-hand side of the screen, there is no reference to a bullet passing through Nermin Divovic's head. It simply says, and I quote: "A child, Nermin Divovic, born 1987 in Sarajevo, was mortally wounded in the head, and Dzenana Sokolovic was seriously wounded."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that is what is in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Of course, I am not competent to say what is in the B/C/S, but I just point that out for purposes of the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, may I just ask the interpreter to interpret that sentence for us, from B/C/S into English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot see the full line in the B/C/S version. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You can see it now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "A sniper bullet was firing at the passers-by at the intersection of Zmaja od Bosne and Franje Rackog Streets in Sarajevo, on which occasion a child, Nermin Divovic, was fatally wounded in the head - he was born in 1987 in Sarajevo - and seriously wounded Dzenana Sokolovic, born 1966 in Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, that's more or less consistent with what was in English. Proceed, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, since we both speak the same language, is what I read correct as I read it?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And as it is written here, is there the words "passed through" in the B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "... passed through the head of the child." It just says part of the word, the first syllable of the word, and the rest is missing. Can I read it? "On that occasion the bullet fired pass the through ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, in these circumstances, I'm minded to ask the CLSS to ask for an authoritative translation of the words. But before I do that, I'd like to find out, what is the direction in which you are going? What is the purpose of your questioning? What do you want to ask the witness about this? I allowed you to question him on the report, but I've yet to see you establish its relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only to establish the truth, whether what the Prosecutor says is true, which trajectory of the bullet was, or what was established on the scene and what the Prosecutor ended in filing criminal charges. I don't think that we need to seek assistance either from the CLSS or from anyone else. Let the witness read and confirm what it says in the B/C/S. The interpreter cannot translate this so precisely as he can read it precisely, and then let the interpreters translate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, I will not follow that course, because we have official authoritative interpreters in this Tribunal, and if it comes to that, then we'll ask the CLSS to provide an interpretation. But the Prosecutor's objection came subsequent to our allowing you to question the witness on this report. So this particular -- are you saying that this particular question raised by the Prosecutor is the point of your examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The point of my examination is the fact that the child was hit first and then the mother and not the other way around, first the mother and then the child. That is the point of all of my work, of my entire effort to discuss this. That is the very point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber will instruct the court deputy to have the CLSS provide an official translation of the relevant passage. Proceed, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, because this witness helped gather evidence, I would like the witness to go back to page 4, if we could just please somehow conceal the fact that he was a member of that team, keep it from being seen on our screens. That is page 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, page 4, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There, Witness. Look at the very end of this long paragraph, the longest on that page. I will read it out to you. "Soon after the incident, two APCs came quickly from the UNPROFOR French Battalion and parked on Franje Rackog Street on the pavement, the registration plates being MFPU 15224 and 8448."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Note: The interpreters don't have the document and can't see the portion that counsel is reading from. We didn't get the numbers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why is that? Let us wait for a few seconds to see whether the interpreters now have it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We have the relevant page now, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that what happened, Witness?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If necessary, I can read that, too, the next paragraph. "There was a blood-stain on the spot where the woman and the boy were wounded which members of UNPROFOR, who later arrived at the site, washed with water and later covered with earth before the arrival of the on-site investigation team." Is that accurate? Is that what happened, sir?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember this particular detail. It wasn't a huge pool of blood. It was just a very small blood-stain. I can't remember whether it was washed away or covered.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm putting it to you, Witness, that UNPROFOR certainly didn't do that. Rather, this was something that was done by the members of your team who then shifted the blame for this to UNPROFOR. That's what I'm putting to you. What do you have to say, sir?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not possible, simply because that's quite a lot to do. It was difficult to stay there for long. It was difficult to carry out any investigations at all, even washing and covering, simply because there was a lot of firing from behind the Metalka building; there was a lot of sniper activity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel. If I understand you correctly, you are implying that the witness was involved in falsification of a public report. I think you have to have a solid foundation for making that allegation, and I'm asking you to provide that foundation to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Either this was falsified, fabricated, by UNPROFOR by destroying evidence or it was someone from the witness's team. It has to be that. However, what I'm suggesting is that UNPROFOR would never do anything like. What I'm suggesting is this was done by the team that was in charge of the investigation and they then shifted the blame for this to UNPROFOR. Be that as it may, whoever destroyed evidence did precious little service to the course of justice and the attainment of truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Counsel, my point is that you do not have the right to imply that the witness has been involved in criminal activity during your cross-examination. And it seems to me that by alleging that the witness was involved in falsification of a public report or mingling with the truth, you are very directly implying that the witness has committed a crime against justice. So unless you have a strong foundation that this was, in fact, the case, I suggest you drop that allegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Harhoff, what I'm suggesting is that this means perverting the course of justice. I am doing that in the clearest possible way and with the greatest possible responsibility, simply because this is the only interpretation that presents itself. And that precisely is my point. It would be even more dreadful if the evidence had been destroyed by UNPROFOR, which is something that I refuse to believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will not be lumbering this witness with another document that the OTP got later on, after everything that had occurred in connection with these events. We'll have sufficient time to deal with that and with the medical certificate that the OTP obtained through their investigators in Sarajevo, having questioned the witness about that. But I will be dealing with that some other time. I do not wish to waste any more of your precious time now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you know anything about the incident that occurred on the 21st of November, 1994, since you worked on sniping incidents, when a shell landed in front of a tram or something? Do you remember that incident where only the driver was injured?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Do you know the range of a rifle-launched grenade?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Since you know nothing about that, I won't be asking any further questions. I do assume, however, that you're familiar with Sefer Halilovic's book; he was the chief of the General Staff. I submitted this for translation. I'm not sure when the translation will be ready. Just several paragraphs. But have you read this book? It was published back in 1998.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't read the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak closer to the microphone. We can barely hear him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, please move closer to the microphone. The interpreters are having trouble hearing you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: A while ago we discussed an investigation that you were involved in. Yesterday you said in reply to a question by the OTP that you had attended or had been involved in a great many investigations; right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was it ever the case in Markale 1 or Markale 2 or any other serious incident, such as the one that occurred at the Simone Bolivar school - you heard about that on TV at least - or when the TV building was hit, were members of the RS army ever allowed to be involved in these investigations?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that this was disallowed. These people were never interested in being part of an investigation, in being involved in an on-site investigation. The circumstances were such that it was entirely illusory for anyone to expect them to come over and be part of an investigation. The town had been under continuous shelling for three years, and after all, we had UN people who were trained for that sort of thing at the time. As far as I know, no request was ever made by anyone from the Serbian side to cross the line and be involved in an investigation. The same question was asked during my testimony concerning Markale 1, but as far as I know, no requests by Serbs were ever made to be part of an investigation. Had a request ever been made, we would have allowed them access.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You would have allowed access to the Serbian side in any of these incidents, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So, then, they would be able to take appropriate steps with regard to people on their side who had committed these acts; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the fact that for security reasons people were IDed on the street, regardless of their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But people were only IDed during the curfew that was in force between 6.00 in the evening and 10.00 in the morning. That's when people were IDed, all ethnicities alike.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In spring-time, morning is day-time; it's no longer night-time.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said between 2200 hours in the morning and perhaps 5.00 or 6.00 -- 2200 hours in the evening and perhaps 5.00 or 6.00 the next morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if there were any Serbs who were IDed and they would walk on for 50 or 100 metres and would be shot by a sniper?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with any such incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You talked about Markale 2 yesterday.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The first thing I'd like to do is show you your own statement, the 21st of September, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The number is D00-0861. Just to save time, I need one paragraph from this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that your statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on to page 2. In paragraph 2 or paragraph 3, rather, you say this: "On-site investigations carried out during the war with regard to mortar incidents normally involved the collection of shrapnel and other remains of ammunition, photographing of a crime scene, making a sketch of a crime scene, and a lot of other technical work." You said that yesterday. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the next paragraph, you say: "Because it was difficult to arrange for proper training during the war, I had not undergone any official training in investigating cases of mortar shelling and artillery shelling." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How, then, were you able at all to establish what the evidence was in these incidents? How could you possibly be a member of these teams that were supposed to establish some sort of truth if you had undergone no sort of training at all?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When one arrives at a crime scene, you find some damage, you find bits of a projectile, a stabiliser fin or something like that, sometimes dum-dum bullets. Whatever ended up there, we would normally find. It was a step-by-step process. We would train ourselves. We would see what this was about. It's no great wisdom to find a piece of iron or any regular-shaped sharp object at a crime scene. So that's what we did. We didn't just investigate major scenes of shelling. We also investigated scenes where there was only material, physical damage, but no loss of human life, where we found a great many pieces like these. So that was one of the things. You had Markale 1, 2, Dobrinja 4, and this was done by people who determined the angle of descent and drew up the appropriate reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We can, therefore, conclude that you knew nothing about the particular features of weapons of any kind.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not something that we had been trained for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: One of the questions you put to the witness was quoting from the report. "Because it was difficult to arrange for proper training during the war, I had not undergone any official training in investigating cases of mortar shelling and artillery shelling." There's just a slight difference in what is in the English. It speaks of formal tuition in the investigation of shelling or mortar incidents instead of training. May I just ask the interpreter to identify that passage and let me know whether the correct translation is "tuition" or "training."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The word in the B/C/S original is actually "teaching," so the interpreter believes it could cut both ways.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, yes. Yes, please proceed, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You then go on to explain how you got your training in this way, and then you say: "I, however, had the opportunity to attend many such crime scenes where I observed UN officers conducting investigations. I observed the methods that they used and I learned how such investigations were conducted." Is that how you eventually learned to do your job, sir?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the UN. It was from the UN that my colleagues and I learned to determine the origin of projectiles, which direction they came from. We learned to distinguish different kinds of marks left by a projectile. So we learned to distinguish between mortar projectiles, missiles, those fired from a gun, artillery projectiles, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Following that type of training, you were involved in the Markale 1 investigation on the 5th of February, 1994. That's what you say in the next paragraph. Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In that same paragraph, I see that you said at the time, on the 5th of February, 1994, "When I arrived at the scene all of those injured had already been taken away." My question is: That was the case on the 5th of February, 1994, and also on the 28th of August, 1995. Wasn't that the case, sir?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can DD00-0861 be admitted as a Defence exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D77, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other document is DD00-0851. This is your statement dated the 25th of April, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not showing the first page to keep your name from being broadcast and to avoid going into private session, unless it is absolutely necessary for you, just in case you don't remember making a statement on the 25th of April, 2006.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did make one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In that case, I'm moving straight to page 2. It's a very brief statement. You see it, sir, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "I don't think there were any other shells landing on the Markale market on the morning of the 28th of August, 1995, or the day before." That's what it says, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that a single shell landed?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a single shell that landed on the Markale area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about any other areas? Were there any other shells landing?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I knew of.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That morning you neither heard nor saw any other shell landing except for the one shell at Markale, did you?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were shells falling every day. It's possible that there were shells landing. I just didn't take notice. It became something that was quite usual. So when the team was called up in relation to Markale 1, that was when I found out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So what about this one shell? What did you hear?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were indoors in our offices. We heard explosions. We couldn't immediately know where the explosions were occurring, which part of town. But this was one that was nearby, so of course we heard the sound of an explosion. When shells were falling, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, if they came in a quick succession, we would be reluctant to leave our rooms, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have photograph number 1 on our screens, 65 ter number 00129.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You see the photograph, sir, don't you? When you arrived at the scene, this is one of the photographs that you took, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's looking from Tito Street in the direction of Bascarsija.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How far from this car was the first shell that landed, if you could show us the point of impact, please.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Here we can see an overturned motorbike. Can you explain to me how it's possible that on this car to the right there is not a single trace of it being hit by anything?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the vehicle of our forensic unit that came there with the kit and the equipment. It's an official car.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now look at the photograph behind you. I don't know exactly what number this photograph is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the question now?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like him to show the photograph on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But in any case, yesterday you showed that there was shrapnel in the wall down there to the right.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can see it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you look now, to the left there is not a single shrapnel, to the far left, not a single shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was impossible for them to be there. This is the exit, and this whole area is where the bodies were. So they were here and the detonation caused injuries and, for the most part, they prevented this area being hit by shrapnel. If you look at this photograph on the monitor, you will see that across -- to the left and upwards, there's major damage, as I explained yesterday. The upper part of the building you see, and I will show to you the dynamics of this damage here and this thing up there with respect to this part where there is very few damaged areas. So the building opposite the market was damaged in its upper part. You see the movement. These are all damage caused by the shrapnel, and that's what I explained yesterday. And if the projectile fell here, the shrapnel dispersed in this direction and caused injuries to the people, and the other shrapnel travel in this direction causing damage to the building, as you can see on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you something different. If you look to the right, there's barely a few pieces of shrapnel. I didn't see a single one on the other side; maybe you did.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The concentration is identical to the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that this type of shell can produce between 3 and 4.000 pieces of shrapnel?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So how is it possible that on this wall, especially on the left where you see blood-stains, of the 4.000 pieces of shrapnel there were just a few? How do you account for that?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason was because 35 people were killed instantly and another 30 succumbed to the injuries later and another 40 people suffered injuries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand. How does that explain why there isn't any shrapnel on the left side, the fact that 35 people were killed and another 30 died later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tried to explain. This was the entrance point where a huge crowd of pedestrians was. It is only logical that these people in this area here -- this is where the bodies were. That's why you don't see any blood, but there were lots of extremities in this area, and it is only reasonable that there is little damage on the wall. However, on the right-hand side, as you can see here and here, there is something, there is a little bit more, which means that the majority of shrapnel was embedded in the bodies of the people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see, okay. Can you just point to a piece of shrapnel on that drawing which is behind you? Because I can't see from here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's a piece. That's actually in the wall.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's in the wall. The impact and a piece of mortar was chipped from the wall which can be better seen in the photograph. You can see that these are fresh traces of mortar being chipped out by a piece of metal or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And so the explanation for less shrapnel being on the left side is that the shrapnel was embedded in the bodies of the victims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, a huge number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, and we collected a lot -- lots of pieces of shrapnel were collected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, we'll have medical evidence on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll get -- we'll get that. We have got the autopsy reports from the victims, and if we weren't planning to put them in, we'll put them in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, the previous witness and everybody else and you also said that between 3 and 4.000 pieces of shrapnel were produced, but there were not 3 or 4.000 people. There were as many people as was said before. Where did, for instance, 2.500 shrapnel go?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know. It doesn't mean that each piece hit somebody. It doesn't mean that the bodies had absorbed all the 3.000 shrapnel. The fact is that we found lots of pieces on the scene, and this has been shown in the photograph. However, where the rest had gone, believe me, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In response to Judge Robinson's question, you explained why these two bicycles were upright and that people were standing in front of them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you also said that the stalls were there with vendors selling cigarettes right on that side.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were no stalls there. People were just standing there and selling various commodities, butter, sugar, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like, if possible, you to show photographs 2, 3, 4, and 5 so that you can see pieces of extremities, which indicates that people were standing there when the detonation held; that the tissue was torn and that accounts for the less damage. However, there was bigger damage to people's extremities. Therefore, I would like for to you show me photographs 2, 3, 5, and 4. If the Prosecutor decides to do so, we can do it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Explain to me: If there were so many people there selling cigarettes and other commodities, where are these items there? Does this mean that the cigarettes and other commodities sold by those people who would die there were removed from the scene?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You can see here a certain quantity of cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But where are these body parts in this photograph? Can you show me at least one?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is a leg, a foot; this is another foot. I also believe that there's another part but it's not very clear. As far as I can remember, those were -- numbers 2, 3, 4, 5, and maybe 6 were the markings of body parts and tissue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, my question was why were the people who were definitely dead removed from the scene before your arrival?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, those who were dead were taken to the morgue. One couldn't leave them lying in the street for two or three hours. And then the wounded were taken care of. It was only natural. I believe that it was only a normal thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Excuse the interruption, but before counsel moves on, can I ask that the photograph on the monitor be saved. I wish to tender that as a Prosecution exhibit either now or during re-direct examination if Mr. Tapuskovic is not going to. And I just want to make sure that it's preserved before the markings go away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the court deputy will see to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to expedite my cross-examination in order to complete it at the end of this session. Can we please look now at photograph number 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please remember to save this before we move to the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This can also be tendered as a Defence exhibit; I have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: It doesn't matter to me. Just so long as it's in evidence one way or the other. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's very cooperative. We will admit it as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D78, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And my thanks to Mr. Tapuskovic for making the offer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, based on the photograph and what you have shown us, would it be fair to say that the characteristics of this shell has been spreading in the form of a circular funnel?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see a better concentration here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm asking you a completely different thing. I put it to you that the spreading caused by this shell and the shrapnel is in the funnel shape, and this is precisely what is shown in this photograph, that they flew upwards into the air. Maybe I'm not right.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you're not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Docherty. I would have forgotten to tender this photograph into evidence. Can we please now move to photograph number 8. Yes, here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the most basic principle and the duty not to tamper with anything at the location where there was an explosion or any such thing happening?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in the course of the investigation. We photographed the scene as we found it. However, since there was a lot of material there, it was impossible to definitely determine the direction of the shell. And as standard procedure, we went on to remove the rubble in order to get an accurate and clear picture of the direction from which the projectile came.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's exactly what I'm asking you. Why did you do anything at all? Why did you clear the scene before the arrival of the investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, no, one cannot start an on-site investigation without the presence of the prosecutor and the judge. They give us the green light to do that, to proceed with the investigation. No one else has the right, without the signal from the judge, to go ahead with any procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, what the counsel was asking you was why did you clear the scene before the investigating judge arrived? The question wasn't whether you started the investigation without the approval of the investigating judge, but why did you clear the scene before the judge arrived? What's the answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. That's not true, that we cleared the scene without the presence of the judge. The judge was there while we were doing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot find this particular statement of yours that you made yesterday, but I do understand your reply. The witness who testified before you, on page 2415, lines 12 to 15, said the first thing would be to locate the stabiliser fin of the shell in order to establish the type of shell. In most cases, we found markings of the manufacturer from Serbia, such as KV, which stands for "Kraljevo" in Serbian. My first question is: Did the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina have these type of shells?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about the weapons of the BH army. I was a police officer, I was doing the police business, and I wasn't a member of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you another thing with regard to the stabiliser. It was retrieved at the distance that you mentioned and indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if we can look at photo 28 -- no, 26 would be better.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that the stabiliser, which is a good indicator of the incoming direction, was flattened.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And that you presumed that there were some individuals who probably moved it, wanting to take it with them as a souvenir.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could easily have happened because there was a commotion and there was a huge need to take care of so many wounded and dead people. However, it is a portable trace, and given that it was between 25 and 30 metres away from the scene, that's where we found it but we never moved it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You know that in Markale 1 this fin was in the crater itself.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was embedded in the asphalt, or, rather, penetrated the thin layer of asphalt and got embedded into the earth underneath and that's where I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's the same surface; it's not far away.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Here you have two or three layers. This is a very busy street, with heavy traffic; heavy-duty trucks pass through it. So it was difficult for it to penetrate the asphalt surface.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Before the event itself, the explosion, there were no trams running down this street, but cars, buses and pedestrians were normally using the street; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I believe that there was some tram service on and off, depending on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So that means that people were not standing on the driving lane; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How is it then possible that there was not a single vehicle, a car, a bus, because as you say it was a busy street, that was not hit? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A motorcyclist was hit. He was passing down the street at that moment. It wasn't such a busy street that you would have a queue of several vehicles. I would say that a couple of vehicles would pass at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All the people were on the pavement, which is barely 1 to 1.5 metres wide.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over 2.5 metres wide.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that the damage, that the flatness of this tail fin, given the quality of the material that it's made of, cannot be deformed by a car? In order to make it look like this, you would need a tractor or something else.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that these fins are so robust. Their thickness is probably between .6 up to a maximum of 1 millimetre, so it is possible for it to be flattened by a bigger vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In order not to dwell on this any longer, for the moment, I'd like to put it to you that, in my opinion, this shell was planted at this specific location and in some possible way then exploded or made to explode.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is absolutely impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And that it was possible that only a few people who happened to be there fell victims to this shell, whereas all the others were brought to the location in the aftermath of the explosion.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where would they have been brought from, Mr. Tapuskovic? I'm trying to understand your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those were the people killed in fighting and subsequently brought to the place where dead people are normally kept before being buried. But most certainly it was impossible for so many casualties. Here now we heard the figure of 60 dead, 30 instantaneously and 30 later, and the indictment speaks about 30, or, rather, 43 dead as a result of this incident. In any case, in view of what I said, I put forward this claim with the conviction that that is what actually happened, and I would not tackle any other incidents other than those that we tackled so far and in which I also believe that the same practice was put in place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When you speak of the place where dead people are normally kept before being buried, do you mean a morgue?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So your case is that they were brought from a morgue and placed at the scene of this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And they were quickly removed from the scene in order to preclude the possibility of establishing the time of death and for other reasons that expert witnesses are going to talk about. I regret that the Prosecutor failed to show us the bodies on the scene while they were still there for you to see how it looked like and to judge whether it is possible for a single shell to cause such devastation, because it normally cannot kill more than ten people, unless all of these people were in one barrel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Your Honour. Thank you. To begin with, what I propose to do is simply tell the Chamber which photographs show severed body parts. I do not plan on displaying those publicly, if that would be acceptable, rather than have the witness look at them one after another. And if the Chamber feels the need to look at these, I will have given the e-court numbers. Is that acceptable, rather than question and answer with the witness? I would simply like to avoid a public display of some truly gruesome photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I don't want to see gruesome photographs, but if there is an evidential point, then you must assess whether you have to show them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I understand. I would draw the Chamber's attention to the following e-court page numbers, from the exhibit that is the portfolio of photographs. E-court page 10 shows a severed human foot with the evidence placard from the police "2" placed beside it, and that will allow you to locate that on the chart that is already in evidence in which those placards -- numbers appear in small circles. E-court page 11 shows a severed human foot; the evidence placard is number 3. E-court page 12, the evidence placard there is number 5. E-court page 14, the evidence placard there is number 4. E-court page 15, the police evidence placard there is number 5. And now I do have just a couple of questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, I regret to say that this informal procedure doesn't meet the evidential requirements. If you are going to ask us to look at the photographs and draw from the photographs an inference that would be favourable to your case, then they must be in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, they are in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: They are in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: They are in evidence. I'm sorry if I was not clear. There was a portfolio of 44 photographs. They were all -- it was 65 ter number 00129. They were all moved. But I published to the Chamber a selection of those photographs, and it is from those photographs that, for example, the montage behind the witness appears, that the photograph of the building appears with the bicycles against it, and so forth. I did not show all 44 photographs, but I did put all 44 in. And the witness has testified that these all photographs he took at Markale on that day, and what I'm suggesting -- I will show them. I do not want to, but I will do it if the Chamber tells me to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. If they are in evidence, that is perfectly proper. But, Mr. Tapuskovic, you must note that these photographs are in evidence. What are the questions that you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Just briefly

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Officer, you recall that when you were being cross-examined, Mr. Tapuskovic asked you a question about where all the cigarettes and other things that the vendors had been selling disappeared to. Do you recall that question and your answer to him?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the items that were found, such as personal documents, were taken by the police and were later returned to those who had been injured or the families of those who had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: If we could, from the portfolio of photographs, see first e-court page 13, I will have a question about that; and then e-court page 33.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not sure how long this re-examination is going to take - I'm not entitled to speak after that, regardless of re-examination - if I could please be excused from the rest of today's hearing, since my learned friend will be taking over the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but let me just say something before you go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before you go, Mr. Tapuskovic, I just wanted to let the parties know of the procedure that I'll follow when the CLSS gives us the translation of that disputed passage. When we have the translation, I will allow the parties to make very brief submissions on it. So you may go, Mr. Tapuskovic. And remember now, we're well past the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have this photograph and then one more, and then I will tender one other item of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Officer, do you see the photograph on the monitor in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Besides blood, what's in the gutter there?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Packs of cigarettes scattered all over the tarmac, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: If we could now see e-court page 33.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Officer, do you see that photograph on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a wallet with an ID card and with lighters. This probably belonged to a person who was selling lighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And this was a photograph taken by you --

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: -- at Markale market on August 28th, 1995.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. This and at least a dozen others like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's all the questions I have for the witness. Before I sit down, I would like to tender - I neglected to do this in my examination-in-chief - the officer's report with the list of the dead. It is 65 ter number 145B. I neglected to tender it at the close of my examination-in-chief, so I ask to do that at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P266, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Now, the photograph that was there before, that's already in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: These are all in evidence, Your Honour. As I say, there were 44 and I think I had the witness actually show and talk about, I don't know, 12 or 13 of them. But all 44 went into evidence after he said that he had looked at all 44 before court and that they were all photographs he had taken at Markale on August 28th, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I asked because that one shows the shrapnel marks which I'm not able to see looking at the drawing which you have at the back of the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And then lastly, for the Chamber's benefit, I was asked about medical evidence of victims absorbing shrapnel, and I have been informed that these were put into evidence already through the two doctors who testified, who put in large volumes of medical reports, and we can highlight for the Chamber which of those relate to Markale market. But they are already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Witness, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for giving it, and you may now leave. We'll adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The next witness, Mr. Whiting, I see is here. Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And you may again, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Could you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: My name is John Jordan.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speakers please observe the pause between questions an answers for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you hear that? You are asked to observe a pause between question and answer in the interests of interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think it will also assist the interpreters, as well as the court reporter, if we do not -- if we take care not to speak too quickly. And also I'm going to ask you to please try to keep your answers as brief as possible, though try to answer the question completely. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I'm going to show the witness his statement, and I have copies also for the Trial Chamber in case you don't have copies with you. Defence counsel, of course, has the statement in English and in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Jordan, is this your statement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to review this statement before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you look, please, at paragraph 45 of your statement. In that paragraph you describe an incident where you saw two snipers in a building in Grbavica. Having reviewed this paragraph, do you want to make a correction to that sentence?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes. There were three, now that I remember right; two on one floor and one on another.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Aside -- excuse me. Aside from that correction, is the statement true and accurate, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If you were to testify here and asked about these matters, is this what you would testify to here in court?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is 65 ter number 2835. I don't believe there is a need to call it up on the e-court, but I'd ask that it be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P267, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Jordan, could you briefly tell us your military background. What military background do you have? That is, before 1992.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: I was on active duty in the United States Marine Corps from 1973 to 1978; I was an enlisted man. I left with the rank of sergeant. My last job was Chief Scout Sniper of the 1st Battalion, 4th Marines.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, sir -- I'm sorry, did you have more --

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: I did some marksmanship instruction training in a number of countries friendly to the US but never held a rank or title in anyone else's military.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And that was after you left the marines in 1978?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Jordan, when did you first go to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when did you leave Sarajevo for the last time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: I believe my last visit was in September or October of 1995, in that area. I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Between those two dates, what's the longest period of time that you were away from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: The longest gap was in the spring of 1995. It was about four or five weeks, and it was in the early spring. I believe I was back in Sarajevo by the beginning of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Other than that period of time, were you essentially in Sarajevo continuously except for brief trips outside of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: I was either in Sarajevo, on my way out to pick up equipment, or on my way back in with equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'd like to show now a brief news clip of a story that is about you, and I hope you're not embarrassed about it, but I think it summarizes what you were doing. We're going to show it on the Sanction so we need to switch over to the Sanction, and I believe by clicking on the e-court button that's how you can watch it. The clip is in English. There is a simultaneous text in B/C/S which will be underneath, and the French booth is already prepared to translate this in French. So if we can show that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Jordan, is that you in the video clip?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes, about a thousand years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That was my next question. What is the date, if you recall, when that was made and broadcast?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: I believe that was March or April of 1993. It would have coincided with the congressional fire an emergency services dinner, which was where it occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In the video clip you make a reference to what people in the hills around the city were doing. Who were you referring to when you say "people in the hills"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: That would be the BSA forces surrounding the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when you say "BSA," what is that a reference to, just so we're clear?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Forces other than the Bosnian government, which was -- who held the town. We just called them the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I just needed what the initials stood for. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Why, in this clip, did you refer to them as the "people in the hills" and not as the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: By that time, March of 1993, I had been there long enough to see things in not so much a black-and-white way, so I didn't want to label a whole country or a whole ethnic group or a whole anybody with a particular label. The anger in the city seemed to be focussed around its peripheries, so that's the way I did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you working or trying to cooperate with the Serb side at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: I had a number of informal meetings with the BSA liaison, a Major Indic and I believe there was a Captain Branic. They were still at the PTT within the city of Sarajevo at the time. And it took a while for them to warm up to the idea of us assisting fire-fighters on both sides of the line. That didn't actually occur for -- probably until the summer of 1993 when I finally got our own vehicle in and I did not have to count on the UN driving me up to Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this clip that was shown be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P268, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Jordan, when you were -- during your time in Sarajevo, did you only fight fires or did you do other things?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: We fought fires. We did what medical emergency response we could. Because we had vehicles and fuel, we tried to assist the locals in any other way we could. We often were involved in everything from body swaps, prisoner exchanges, assisting other NGOs that had no mobility to transport everything from supplies to water. It's not so much a European tradition, but in the US, firemen typically don't say no to anything. We try to justify our existence and people's tax dollars by doing anything the community needs. The local fire departments did not do medical; we tried to change that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Would you respond to shelling and/or sniping incidents?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes, we would do this both in an after-the-fact situation, in other words, if we heard a shelling, we would respond to the sound. If somebody called us and said somebody was shot, we would also respond. We would also pre-position equipment and personnel in areas where, on any given day, snipers were particularly active. They came out a lot in nice weather. People came out, made it a target-rich environment, and the snipers got busy. So we would pre-position in areas of known locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber where your fire station was located in 1994 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: By then we were located in the centre of municipal Sarajevo, in Cengic Vila. We were on a small off-road just off the main road, 6th Proletariate Brigade Boulevard, in what was a former supermarket which we turned into the UN's first fire station.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was that in an area under Bosnian army, Bosnian government control, or under the control of the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: That would be under Bosnian government control.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where in Sarajevo did you do your work? What neighbourhoods? What areas?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: We responded to fires and medical emergencies everywhere from the Vogosca automobile plant all the way over to Lukavica, but the vast majority of our responses were in the area, I would say, east of the station and within Bosnian government-controlled areas to the east of us. That seemed to be where the majority of our responses were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you -- I'm sorry. Could you look, please, at paragraph 11 of your statement. In that paragraph you state that you began receiving applications from volunteers from all over the world. Did you have volunteers in your organisation from countries other than the United States; and, if so, can you tell us which countries?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Because of media coverage and coverage in different fire and emergency medical trade magazines, we began very early in 1993 to get resumes from fire and emergency medical personnel in different countries. The number of countries, I could not tell you, as far as how many we received, because the pile of resumes was about as tall as I am. The folks that we did deploy to Sarajevo were American, Canadian, British, French, German, Czech, Lebanese, and one Spanish kid. I think that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Please look at paragraph 15 of your statement. In that paragraph, and it also occurs in paragraph 32 of your statement, you explain what you would do if you went to the scene of a fire or another incident and there was shooting at you. Could you please just briefly describe for the Trial Chamber what the procedure was that you would follow if you went to a location and you were coming under fire. What would you -- what steps would you take?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: It is important to first describe the genesis of that procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Briefly.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: The UN had troops in Sarajevo; it did not have fire service personnel, other than at the airport. The UN was not specifically protecting local fire-fighters on other side of the confrontation line. The fire-fighters on both sides were being wounded and killed. We decided the first thing that had to be addressed was their safety. We convinced the UN to protect the local fire-fighters in a symbiotic way, because once the UN agreed to protect the firemen, the firemen then agreed to respond to fires in UN structures. So basically they were finally doing a little good instead of ignoring each other. So the procedure evolved to where we knew the city better than UN troops. UN troops' typical deployment was 90 days. They operated in convoys, strict routes. They didn't know the alleys, the back streets, the fastest way from point A to point B. So we would go to the fire with the locals, whichever side. Then we would determine if the building that was on fire was being shot at. If it was, our first order of business would be to determine if there was a reason the building was being shot at. In other words, if there was a man on the roof firing uphill or downhill with a gun, in that environment he got shot back at and the people who lived there just had to endure it. If we arrived and there was a building on fire, gun-fire going into it and no military activity in the building, coming from the building, then we would contact UN headquarters. We would give the UN military observers a grid coordinate of where the gun-fire was originating from and a description of the weapon. At that point, the UN would look for the UN military observer who was responsible for that particular area. He would then contact the local force commander and tell him that, Look, we have UN firemen in the building; you're shooting at a building that has no military significance; please stop --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please speak slower for interpretation, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I believe that this is a bit too fast and the interpretation into French and in B/C/S is difficult because the witness is speaking too fast. So it's difficult for us to follow the translation, so could the witness please speak slower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we all heard the request of the interpreter and Ms. Isailovic. Speak slower.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you should be bringing this answer to a close now. Generally, I prefer short answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I take responsibility for this one, Your Honour, because the question I asked for, really, a long answer. So I'll break it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Once you called the UN and told them the grid reference where the gun-fire was coming from and the description of the weapon, what would they do, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: They would attempt to contact a local commander and ask him to cease fire based on our report that the fire was in a civilian structure with no military significance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what then would happen? What would be the result, if any, of that call?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: In the vast majority of cases, the gun-fire ceased.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And to your recollection, when this procedure was followed, were the grid references from which the fire was coming on the Bosnian Serb army territory, Bosnian government territory, or both?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
