utterances.text: Bosnian Serb army territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber how many times you went to a location and you determined that it was a military target?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Well under 5 per cent. Rarely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look at paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry. What was the criterion that you used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Uniformed armed military personnel within the fire ground, storage supplies, like a lager or bivouac area, or gun-fire coming from within the fire ground, the building on fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we turn to paragraph 19, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In this paragraph you describe an incident when you were hit in the chest with a bullet in November of 1994. I just have a few brief questions about this incident. Did it happen during the day or at night?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Daylight.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How do you know that -- you say that it came from a Serb position. How do you know that? How did you determine that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Because I knew where the Serb positions were in relation to where I was standing. I know where the bullet hit me and where I went after that. The bullet had to come from positions occupied by the BSA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: At the moment that you were hit by the bullet, were you out in the open or were you somehow not visible?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: I had momentarily exposed myself, moving from point A to point B in the course of fighting a fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And can you describe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Were there any other troops in the area, apart from the Serb troops? Any Bosnian government troops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were some within 50 metres of where I was at, because there was a trench line nearby. But I was wearing fireman's equipment and I was carrying a rolled hose. I was fighting a fire in a building occupied by civilians on one side and, unfortunately, military on its back side. That was the nature of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why are you able to rule out the possibility that the shot came from those forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were all hiding, and the shot came from well above me. It hit me at a down angle and drove me to the ground. And I believe I might have heard the muzzle blast; it was that close. It was a single, well-aimed round from a position above me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Jordan, can you describe briefly what you were wearing, what your fireman outfit looked like.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: I was wearing a typical fireman's ensemble, but it was coloured blue, much like UN colours, with glossy white reflective patches, a blue shiny white fireman's helmet with "UN" on it, and not camouflaged in any way. My flakjacket was also blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look, please, at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This blue uniform, Mr. Witness, was that the UN colour or was it the U.S.? Wasn't it going to be a little bit confusing and wasn't there a possibility that you could confuse it with the military or the police uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. My uniform could not be confused with military or police by any rational individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Why do you say that, Mr. Jordan? Can you just be more specific?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: It was not camouflaged in any way, shape or form. Again, it was like the UN blue, very bright, glossy white reflective patches on it so that one sees one's partners in the smoke. My blue fireman's helmet was also a shiny gloss blue helmet, nothing camouflaged about it. The BSA firemen wore green uniforms; the Bosnian government firemen wore black. There was no way to mistake me for anything other than what I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you turn, please, to paragraph 22 of your statement. In the middle of that paragraph, you say: "The majority of fire against us came from the Bosnian Serbs." Then in the next paragraph you describe an incident that occurred in July of 1995 where you suspected that mortars that landed around you were fired from the Bosnian Muslim side. My question is this: Aside from that incident that you describe in paragraph 23, were there any other occasions where you believe or suspect that fire came on you from the Bosnian Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Not while on their territory, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did it occur while you were not on their territory; and, if so, where?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: On one occasion we were on a hill above the south-eastern part of Sarajevo. We were fighting a fire in a home on BSA territory, and a couple of random rifle rounds were fired at us and it just stopped. We never got a grid. We never ceased fire operations. A couple of random rounds and then it stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did it happen on any other occasion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Not that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you ever hear -- did you ever witness or hear of Bosnian government forces either shelling their own people or firing sniper fire on their own people?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Those rumours circulated constantly among UN personnel, media personnel, and particularly among folks on the BSA side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did you yourself, during your time there, lend any credence to those rumours? Did you believe them?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: I didn't think the Bosnian government forces had the ability to pull that off without everyone knowing it, on the one hand. On the other hand, if they were doing it to elicit sympathy or some reason, it was obviously a failed policy because the sympathy they were looking for never showed up. So those are the two reasons, I think, there was nothing to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you say in paragraph 22 that "the majority of fire against us came from the Bosnian Serbs, usually high ground or from a building known to be under their control," can you tell the Trial Chamber how it is that you determined that? How would you know that fire against you was coming from the Bosnian Serb side? What things would you take into account to make that determination?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: We had to be alive to help people, so it was our job to constantly monitor what buildings were under whose control and presented what manner of threat to our operations on a daily basis. I don't like to use the expression "common knowledge," but one gets to know the neighbourhood they live in and the demographics of any given neighbourhood. We had to know the violence potential in any given neighbourhood. That was our job.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you have explained to the Trial Chamber how it is that you knew who controlled what areas, but when fire was coming on you, either sniper fire or shelling, how would you determine that that firing was coming from the Bosnian Serb areas, when you made that determination? What sort of factors would assist you in making that determination that that's where the fire was coming from?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: We employed the same tactics and techniques of military forward observers with the difference being we tried to call fire off as opposed to calling fire down on a target. Basically, we used the same skills one teaches military forward observers to identify targets. We used them to identify threats and pass that information on to the UN. Same tools, same skill-set, different intent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But I'm going to ask you to be a little bit more specific. Just imagine -- just try to cast your mind back to occasions when you were under fire, either gun-fire or shelling. What specific things would you look for to tell you where the fire was coming from? How would you make that determination? Maybe it seems like a basic question to you --

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: -- but it would assist us. How can you tell where shooting or shells are coming from?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: When you see three men on an anti-aircraft gun 2.000 metres away and they are pointing the gun at a building and shooting, and you know where they are on the map and you can see them loading the gun and firing the gun, you can see them. That was it half the time. At night it would be based on muzzle flashes. But most of the time it was direct observation. If we did not know, we did not say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The incident that you describe in paragraph 23, can you tell us where that occurred?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: We had responded to a fire in a single family dwelling on the Bosnian government side of the line, right near the Jewish cemetery, which was an area of what we called "high incident" because of proximity of the opposing forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How close to the front line was that location, if you know?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: I would say we were within 100 metres or so of the area between the forces, that area expanding and contracting as the opposing forces' lines approached each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Please look at paragraph 29. You describe seeing mortar tubes well dug in on the Serb side. Are you able to tell us specifically where that was on the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: The hill road from -- on the way to Lukavica, you could go up -- you would be on the high ground above the south side of Sarajevo. That road was dotted with positions, bunkers, where men lived. It was just back from the front line. But there were support weapons in those positions in a number of places with vistas of Sarajevo below it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And can you describe what a mortar dug in looks like. What would you observe in terms of the mortars dug in?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Well, one can set up a portable mortar anywhere. But when one wants to be really accurate, you put it in a position and you put out things that look like a surveyor's kit, what we call triangulation equipment - aiming stakes, levels, little things that make what you're trying to do more accurate. We would see some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And just to be clear, you saw that on the Serb side in the location that you identified.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes, a number of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In paragraph 35 you say: "I saw the Bosnian Muslims use a portable mortar from the hospital in late 1994." First of all, do you know which hospital that was?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: I always mixed the hospitals up. It was the one that was in the compound -- not the one that the media always focussed on. Pardon me, I always mixed the two hospitals up. It was the one that had like a complex of buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, there is the State Hospital building, which is kind of a white building that stands in the middle of the city, and then there's the Kosevo Hospital, which is something of a complex. Are you able to --

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: That would be it, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, I believe that Mr. Whiting is testifying. Maybe the witness can just answer the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting, that was a little leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I was trying to give the choice of the two hospitals in the city, which I don't think there is any dispute about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In any event, in your own words, why don't you describe the hospital and its location.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: There are two hospitals in Sarajevo. One was a single cube-like structure sticking up on its own, much photographed by the media because of the damage to it. The other hospital was in a complex that had other buildings around it, in more like a university setting. Again, pardon me, I always mixed the two up, but I know which one I saw the Bosnian government forces fire a mortar from, and that was the one that was complex-like.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And are you able to tell us, if can you recall, how they are situated in relationship to each other by direction? Which one -- is one to the north, to the west, to the east, or is that something you cannot recall?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes, I can recall that. The much-photographed one was not far from the main drag. It was east of the former Tito barracks. The other one kind of up in the back, going up towards the Olympic stadium, kind of up in that neighbourhood. I could find them both on a map, if I had to, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I actually think you've been sufficiently clear, so I'm not going to take the time to do that, but thank you. Now, how many times -- you say you saw the Bosnian Muslims use a portable mortar from that hospital in late 1994. How many times did you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: I saw it once and thought I heard it happen on a couple of other occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Turn, please, to paragraph 38, where you talk about air bombs, one of the paragraphs you talk about air bombs, and you say: "There is no way the Bosnian Muslims could have had something that big without us knowing about it." Can you explain that statement, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: By "us," I mean everybody. A weapon that large would be the size of a small drilling rig. You could not use it without the whole neighbourhood knowing it. It wasn't a question of myself and my personnel being so well informed. It would be the equivalent of a group of guys driving a large drilling rig, setting up in a neighbourhood, launching something and nobody seeing anything. I do not believe that was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Look, please, at paragraph 41, where you describe the corps headquarters at Lukavica. How many times did you go to that headquarters in Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: At least half a dozen. We visited it before -- we usually visited Lukavica -- before visiting the local firemen or meeting with someone in Pale, we would usually stop in Lukavica, just to stop and say hello before we went about our business.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In paragraph 44 you describe an incident where UNPROFOR soldiers came under attack where you were present. Do you know, were you able to tell, on that occasion where the firing came from?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes. We were on our way to the US embassy for a country team meeting prior to the arrival of President Carter, and a spasm of shooting started in front of the Holiday Inn that included small arms, automatic weapons, a couple of mortar rounds, a couple of RPGs. Just a 10-, 15-minute flare of random violence that came and went.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But my question was: Were you able to determine where that fire came from?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes. It was coming from the BSA-occupied buildings to the south of the museum.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you -- now this is a question that does not pertain to a specific paragraph in your statement. Did you become aware of a tunnel in the area of the airport?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And could you just briefly describe that. Did you yourself go into that tunnel?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes, five times altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you just briefly describe it for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: The tunnel could have benefitted from a good engineer; I would recommend Vietnamese myself. It was particularly narrow; half the time full of water; one-way traffic; had a small rail system to put carts on that constantly fell apart; lights that constantly went out; a ventilation system that was inadequate. A ratty little water-filled tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Another topic. Did you ever hear of Bosnian government sniping positions at the museum?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: The Bosnian government maintained sniping positions opposite their protagonists just about everywhere in Sarajevo. Never heard of them in the museum itself but out back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of those snipers at the back of the museum firing on their own people, that is, firing on people on the Bosnian government side?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that all the time but never saw it myself, nor do I believe it to have occurred, since that was one of the areas where we would pre-position ourselves quite often. And if I'd seen or believed that to be occurring for one second, I would have pulled my people out and informed authorities that that's what was happening, just like I did with the mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Finally, I'm just going to show you a few brief clips and perhaps one document to finish up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could switch to the Sanction and look at clip number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And I'm going to ask you, sir, when this occurred and maybe one or two other questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Jordan, to your recollection, when did that occur?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: That was December 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And approximately where in Sarajevo is that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: It was a residential district just north of the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: On that occasion, did the -- after the building collapsed and while the rescue was going on, was there any -- did the rescuers come under any shelling or sniping?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: They did not come under sniper fire. There was a lengthy inconsistent artillery, i.e., rockets in this case. It was a rocket that brought the building down. The rescue of the child would not have been possible had we not been in contact with the Lukavica barracks via PTT, who, when we told them that it was a residential area, that there were children trapped, could they please cease-fire, they did. And that's when the UN troops were sent up to assist us with their heavy equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this clip be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P269, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, did you shoot that video or was it the UN?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe the video was given to us by whichever international journalist happened to shoot it. I cannot say I remember who.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we look at the next clip. It's clip number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic is on her feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honour. Maybe something needs to be clarified, because I have only one video clip on my list and I believe that this is the clip that we've just seen. In order to be able to refer back to the evidence, is this the same video with another 65 ter number? And will it have various numbers afterwards as exhibits? For the future, in order to be able to refer back to these documents, I need some clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. These are all clips from one video, and we've isolated clips. And as I play them and move them into evidence, they will get new exhibit numbers -- I mean they will get, I'm sorry, individual exhibit numbers. If we could look at the next clip. It's clip number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Jordan, do you know when this event occurred that is in this video clip?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: That incident is from the fall of 1994. I believe Trevor Gibson, one of our personnel there, got shot in the butt that night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Who was speaking in it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The gentleman speaking is Mark Anderson. He was Acting Deputy Chief of GOFRS at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: GOFRS being your NGO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Jordan, it says that this occurred -- in the video clip it says it occurred at 4.30. Do you know if that's 4.30 in the morning or 4.30 in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As Exhibit P270, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And finally the last clip is clip number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Jordan, were you yourself present when that occurred, when what we see on the video clip occurred?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were men who worked under you, for your organisation, present?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did they tell you at the time what had happened there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes. They were in a -- in front of the museum. It was a nice day, so the snipers were active. Prior to this incident, a number of people had been shot and wounded, so we set up to deal with any further casualties. The young boy who was killed had just been talking to one of my fire-fighters, Todd Bayly, and had asked him for candy. Todd told him told, "Nema bombons," no candy, and he walked away with his mother. And within a couple of metres, a single round killed the child and wounded the mother. That's when the boys pulled the ambulance between the source of the gun-fire and the child to recover his body, and later on evacuated the wounded mother and the little girl.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did the people on location tell you anything about where the source of fire came from, if they knew, if they had any information about that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes. Again, it was a nice day, and that seemed to bring out the snipers. So the building behind the museum across the river, it was just an active day for them. Again, not to be redundant, but on nice days, the snipers came out. That's just the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did you speak with Todd Bayly in the past few days and confirm your recollection about what he told you about what had occurred there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes. It was the first time I had spoken to Todd in ten years. My recollections were correct. The impetus in calling Todd was just to answer a technical question about where the boy was standing, to the left or right of the mother, which, to me, was moot. But I thought it might help the Court in some manner, so we gave Todd a shout.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And was Todd able to answer that question?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: I don't remember. Was he? Yes or no? I don't know. I forgot.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this clip please be put into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P271, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look now at 65 ter number 2960. And if we could -- it's the same picture on both sides. If we could blow it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Does this photograph pertain to the incident that we just saw the clip about?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes. It was shot by an Associated Press photographer who was on scene. It shows Todd Bayly of Canada right next to our vehicle. The other gentleman is Trevor Gibson of Scotland. They have just pulled away from the museum and put the -- that's our armoured ambulance between the child and the gun-fire. You can see, I believe, the crosswalk is still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what is the building that you can see behind there in the upper right of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: That would be the museum.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this photograph be admitted into evidence, please. I'm sorry, one last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think you have already addressed this, but just to be clear, what is the significance of where the vehicle is located?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: The vehicle is between the child and the man who killed him, straight down that street to the high buildings controlled by the BSA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Have you finished or you want it admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Admit it, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did he say what GOFRS means?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I believe it's in the statement, but he can say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It means Global Operation Fire Rescue Services, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we'll admit this as Exhibit P272.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And finally, I've gone a little bit over time, but with the indulgence of the Court, just one last document. It's 65 ter number 2961.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recognise this?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: It's basically an "ata boy" from General Rose, a complimentary letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P273, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jordan. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Jordan. I'm Branislava Isailovic, an attorney with the Paris Bar, and I'm defending General Milosevic, accused here in these proceedings. And with you, I'm going to ask you a few questions. I'm sure my colleague told you about the procedure. We're going to examine you about -- especially on your statement, the statement that you gave to the OTP on August 22nd, 23rd, 24th, 2006. A number of questions have already been dealt with. And I'm also going to use a number of documents that have to do with the statement. So, first and foremost, Mr. Jordan, I would like to start with this organisation of yours. It's an NGO; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you right, this NGO is under American law, right, was established under American law?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: That would be correct, for tax purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And regarding authorisations to perform missions on the Bosnian territory, it depended on the Bosnian government, I guess.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes. We needed their permission to operate in their areas of control and BSA permission to operate in their areas of control.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: My question is on the administrative procedures that you had to go through. I guess that, according to Bosnian law, you had to register your company with some kind of authority. Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: I had dropped off paperwork about our organisation with the Bosnian government a number of times. Their administrative procedures are -- how can I say? If I can't say anything nice, I probably shouldn't say. But that would probably best describe their administrative procedures.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And this administrative procedure, was there some kind of official document about your NGO that eventually was drafted or something? Was there any kind of official paper?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: There had to be at one point or another, but because we were under UNHCR and because we carried UNHCR ID, it was kind of a blanket thing. Even though the Bosnian government did afford us with ID in the early days before we became part of the UN, a lot that occurred during UNHCR and UNPROFOR operations in this area was ad hoc. They were doing things they had never done before, and from what I've learned, they have done things they have never done since.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So to try and help us continue with other evidence, could you tell us exactly when exactly you -- when exactly you became part of the UNHCR? When did you come under their auspices?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: The UNHCR had two levels of auspices. They gave out UNHCR ID cards to hundreds of organisations from 1992 to 1995. This was, in effect, the UNHCR telling the warring parties that these organisations are legitimate. The next level was what was called implementing partner status. An organisation received implementing partner status with the UNHCR when it accepted funding from them. We had operated on our own from November 1992 until, I believe it was, March 1993, the first time the UN offered us funding. That did not actually occur until, I believe, May or June, when the paperwork was worked out. At that point, GOFRS, which was our organisation, implemented what we came to call the UN Fire an Emergency Medical Service, UN Fire EMS. I'm not sure anyone told Boutros-Ghali, but that is the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jordan, on this last question regarding all this, on the videos I noticed that you were still -- you still had your NGO emblems. Was that true, after you became part of UN?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Our uniforms, station uniforms, if you will, were the dark blue ones with white "UN Fire EMS" on the pocket and "GOFRS" on your shoulder, the equivalent to when WHO puts its logo on aircraft. Even though it's part of the UN, UNHCR is part of the UN, they put "UNHCR" on their aircraft. Basically in that venue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And financially, did you have donations? Did this NGO get donations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes, we received donations from the international fire-fighting community, primarily the US as far as dollars went. Different European fire-fighting agencies donated many vehicles and equipment which was compatible with that which the locals on both sides used in Sarajevo. We delivered three trucks in one day once; a red one for the Bosnian government, a green one for the Bosnian Serbs, because their equipment was green, and a white one for UNHCR, all from Europe and compatible with the equipment in use.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: These donations to the two sides, as well, to the UNHCR, were they -- was it donated to your organisation and then you gave them, turned them over, or how did the parties eventually get those trucks?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: We didn't give anything to the UNHCR. We gave everything to the locals on both sides based on need. Say, for example, on one occasion we had, like, 400 pairs of boots come in. We actually divided them up by size in the Sarajevo Bosnian government firehouse, the old one on Jablanica Street, and the local firemen there helped us sort it out. And I think we took 100 sets of boots over to Grbavica because they had less firemen than the locals. It was a question of dividing stuff up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, we're going to take the break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jordan, let's continue. Let's go back to what we were talking about before the break. You did not show the funding act of your NGO, nor did you show the balance -- the balance sheet of your NGO to the Prosecutor; am I right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: That would be correct. Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have them at home?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: I don't think so. Anything ten years old -- I haven't been in the States much since then, so I don't think I have got them laying around. Maybe one of the other guys does.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's move to something you mention in your statement, something you also discussed today regarding your military career. You joined the US Army when you were 17; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: No, ma'am. I joined the US Marines when I was 17.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I see. I don't know much about this, but isn't that part of the US Army?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: No, ma'am. It's actually -- pardon me. It's actually within the department of the navy.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. I have just received an explanation from my French interpreter. But you were a platoon head or sniper, as a sniper?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. My last job was Chief Scout Sniper of an infantry battalion. That fell within the STANO platoon, STANO meaning surveillance, target acquisition, and night operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But am I right in saying that from 1993 -- I'm sorry, no. 1973, yes, that's what I meant. When you were 17, you started your military career, so to speak, as a marine or as a soldier at least.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood correctly your statement, you specialise in sniping.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And your task in Sarajevo had to do with fire, and of course this could be understood in different ways. You were a fire-fighter, so you were fighting against fire and fires; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And to be more specific, in paragraph 15, and I believe this is a paragraph you discussed with Mr. Whiting a moment ago, paragraph 15 of your statement, you referred to this other type of fire, mainly shooting. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And in a way, your task in Sarajevo was also to fight snipers, if I understood correctly.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: It did evolve into that, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jordan, were you aware of the Anti-Sniping Agreement which was signed by the warring factions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: I had heard of it, yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And did you know that the French Battalion, I believe, was in charge of this anti-sniping fight?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: I know they were in charge of it at one time. I believe the duty rotated among UN forces. Whoever had reaction duty would respond to sniping, but we found the vast majority of UN forces reluctant to actually do what they said they were going to do on paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In a sense, what they were supposed to do on paper was done by you in practice.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Our mission was to assist the fire-fighters on both sides in whatever way we could. We found that they were very -- on both sides, they were very competent fire-fighters, they used similar equipment, but their biggest need after equipment was protection and fuel. So it fell to us as part of the overall job.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood, when you arrived in Sarajevo, you had a specific task which was, in fact, to protect fire-fighters. Wasn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: No. My first -- when I first arrived in Sarajevo, it was to see what they needed. I was quite surprised to find out that the primary need of fire-fighters on both sides was protection. I was ignorant of UN operations. I had never been involved in one, so I thought the UN was protecting the firemen and didn't find out until I got there that they really weren't.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I was driving at when I asked the question. You realised then that UNPROFOR was not protecting these people; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Not consistently, ma'am, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And specifically in this case of fire-fighters who were just doing their job; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes. In the course of doing their normal duties, firemen on both sides would be targeted and were taken casualty.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And at that stage your mission, so to speak, changed a little bit and became more a fight against snipers than the protection of fire-fighters. Am I right in saying so?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: It was an element. We still did an awful lot of fire-fighting, medical, and transport of supplies. We did an awful lot of talking with both side to keep lines of communication open, and that minimised the violence against both sides. The UN protection order of September 1993 drastically reduced the violence against both sides' firemen. When we did have to respond, we did so with reluctance, not relish. It became a focus of people, like the media, but we never considered it the biggest part of what we were trying to do. We tried to reduce the violence in many ways.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 15 of your statement, a moment ago you referred to this procedure; I'll call it the spotting procedure, when you were trying to spot snipers.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Very often you located snipers and then you would convey that information to UNPROFOR; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes, that was what we tried to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You see, before this Trial Chamber, we've seen a lot of sitreps, or situation reports, emanating from UNPROFOR. I myself did not realise that your mission was in fact defined on those situation reports. Do you know more about this?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: I am not at all surprised that there may be little to no documentation of exactly what our job evolved into. Even with regards to the September 1993 paperwork from UNPROFOR, because UNPROFOR troops in Sarajevo generally only spent 90 days there, there was a constant rotation and there was -- in the military, one makes an effort to pass on information to the person who relieves him. This was severely lacking in UN operations. We were constantly having to reintroduce ourselves to every new UN unit that came in, and some of them told us right to our face, No, the French wrote this; we're not going to do it. So we just handled it ourselves and no one ever told us not to.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You did it of your own accord, then.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Not so much of our own accord. When the system broke down because of UN reluctance to do what it said it was going to do, we merely exercised our right of self-defence. We never got involved in what I would call real estate deals, i.e., combat, trading lives for real estate, to control a piece of ground. That was never something we did. We were also careful not to allow either side to manipulate us into being a force multiplier for them. We were very careful of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. So you also did some stand-by duty on a number of locations. On the days when the weather was good, you said that you were on stand-by duty.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes. Again, different days snipers would be active.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Excuse me, we're getting French on the English channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are getting French.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Any English now on the English channel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, there was a little glitch.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So those people were people belonging to your NGO. Those people were on stand-by duty. It was your staff.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes. When we saw the violence level increase in any one area for whatever reason, we would pre-position folks there to reduce our response time to casualties.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Who made those decisions regarding the intensity of combat? Who was there to estimate the level of combat violence so that you would go to -- be on stand-by duty?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: The casualties made that decision. When we heard somebody had been shot and needed assistance, we would respond. If, in the course of taking that person to the hospital, we found that another person had been shot in the same location, it was the indicators. It was -- it was the violence equivalent of looking up at the clouds and deciding it's probably going to rain today, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So, if I understood you right, the source of your information were mainly the casualties that you encountered when you were going to the hospital. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: No. We wouldn't be going to the hospital and then seeing casualties. If there were multiple casualties in a given area, that is a good indicator that the snipers are busy. So we would then -- instead of going back to our station after dropping of a casualty, we would go back to the area where the casualties seemed to be turning up.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but those casualties, did they come to see you, or was it you who went to see them? That was the question.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: In the majority of cases, we responded to the casualties. We had a few, what we call, walk-in patients at the fire station, but the majority of folks who had been shot were in no position to walk. So we would go to them, particularly if they were wounded in an exposed position, because our ambulance was armoured. The locals had no armoured ambulance.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jordan, can we agree to say that the place where -- this museum that we mentioned earlier was part of those hot spots, if I could say so?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: That would be entirely correct, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like my case manager to display photograph 2819 in the 65 ter list. It's already been tendered as P88, has already been tendered into evidence as P88. Could the usher please come and help Mr. Jordan to show him how to work the electronic pen.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jordan, here on the screen we have an aerial view of Sarajevo, a part of Sarajevo. Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Can you find your way in this photograph? Do you know what is on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: It's relatively familiar to me. Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Let's start with Miljacka? Do you see it on this photograph, the river Miljacka?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: One cannot actually see the river, but it's in the line of trees between the museum and this line of flats here. It runs right along here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please mark this with an M, like the river, Miljacka, M.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now, the bottom part of the picture, is this Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Part of it, yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Could you show us the delineation of Grbavica. You said it's only part of it. Could you show us where it is. Show us where Grbavica is in relation to that line.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. I believe the actual part of Grbavica is the low part down here, here and here, that way, I think, with that building being split because it was split among the forces. The higher ground actually, I think, has a different name, if I remember right. But this was Grbavica and it kind of stuck out from the kidney-shaped rest of the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. So when you're saying there is a split building, could you expand on this, please, and mark it.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: I believe it was this building right here, where I have this other line, that actually had both sides' forces in it at one time. It was not really an area where we would go because there was no civilian activity there. We did work up to the front lines on a number of occasions where there were residences near the front lines. But this whole area here was basically a no-go area for us because there was nothing but troops down around there and that wasn't our end.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Could you be more specific on those troops? Where were they stationed? Could you tell us where they were located, those troops?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Again, we didn't concern ourselves with the actual specifics. We knew the areas they were in. For example, in front of the museum up here is where we would position ourselves to protect folks moving up and down the main drag, because they would be fired on -- this was probably the busiest zone right here. But to go down where the troops were actually looking at each other was not our end of it, so we did not do that. Again, we had no business right where the troops were facing each other. We only came in proximity to them where maybe a building was partially occupied by military.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But could you show us that place on that photograph. We can't see it here. What part of the photograph are you talking about when you're saying that there were troops? I haven't really understood where those troops were.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: It was my understanding that the Bosnian government had troops on their side of the river here, and I know that the BSA forces occupied some of these higher structures because that's where they would fire from. Presumably, the Bosnians engaged them from back here, but I couldn't see that because we stayed up here. Again, we had no business running around back here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jordan. Could you mark where you put the several lines. Put "ABiH" for, you know, the Bosnian government army.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, earlier you mentioned snipers who were behind the museum, in the back of the museum. Could you show that exactly on the map, on this photograph. I'm sure that you see the museum in the buildings, so could you tell us where the snipers were, those who were in the back of the museum?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: I could not, ma'am, because I never went back there. That, again, was not our end. There were no civilians living in those structures, and if -- if the military had any casualties there, they evacuated them themselves because we didn't. We were up here where the civilians were, the front line. Again, while there were some houses where the back of the house was the front line and the other side of it was where civilians lived, that's where we would get in proximity. But this is not an area where any of my guys would be messing around, unless he wanted to get fired.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So if you could please mark the split building with a letter. Put a D, as in "Daniel," on that split building, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Is a circle good enough? That's the building I seem to remember was split.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: On this photograph, do you see other buildings that would be below the Miljacka but that were on territory controlled by the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Well, again, it's not the area we went, but one can assume that since the river was the boundary here to some point over here - and again I wouldn't know where that is right over here - it would be -- I mean, one could assume that the Bosnian government had folks in buildings along here, but I can't say I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: We'll come back to that. But before tendering this photograph, could you please tell me on this photograph the place where the incident we mentioned occurred, you know, where the little boy was killed with his mother.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: At that intersection.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please place a number 5 here, because this is our incident number 5. Maybe draw a line to the circle so we can see that the 5 has to do with that circle at the intersection.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And now this street that runs parallel to the river and that goes in front of that yellow building, do you know that avenue?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: I don't know the name of it, ma'am, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But isn't it the avenue that used to be called "Sniper Alley"? Isn't that the one?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Ma'am, in my experience, there were a number of places referred to as "Sniper Alley." A very large lack of consistency with names of things in the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: First, before we actually tender this photograph, could you tell me if you see two high-rises that are in the top right of this photograph?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. It would be the Unis towers, I believe they were called.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: According to your memory, did BiH snipers -- were BiH snipers located in those towers?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: I think it would be correct to assume so. Can't say I saw any. I think it's a lousy sniping position, to tell you the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Could you mark these high-rises with the letter U, letter U, like "Unis."

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see the government's building?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, the old parliament.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And could you place a letter G on this building.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: G, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: The other building that's not quite as high, was it also part of the government building, as far as your memory goes?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: I don't remember, ma'am, if that was actually part of the government complex or something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether BiH snipers were located in the government building?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: I don't know. I never saw any shooting from there. Our relationship with the snipers on both sides was restricted to whether or not they engaged us. We didn't seek a relationship with them and didn't get to know them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to tender this annotated photograph into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D79, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jordan --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Counsel, while we are still at that photo, could you please ask the witness to explain just why he thought the Unis building would be a bad sniping position.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, according to what I heard in my headphones, I didn't hear really well the witness, but I believe what he said was quite the opposite. But I can put the question again to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jordan, a moment ago we talked about the Unis towers. You put the letter U on those buildings. Judge Harhoff wanted me to put the question to you again: Was this place a good sniping location or not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Personally, I wouldn't use it because it's a tall, cold, isolated building, and if you tried to take a shot out of it, anybody within 2.000 metres and a good thermo-sight would know you were moving about the building. It's actually too high, in my opinion. It should be a little closer to the ground with access in and out. The building being isolated, largely glass all the way around, no, I wouldn't pick it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is a glass building now. But you could have used other storeys in the building, less high than the top of the building.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: The idea of the sniper way up in the building, the sniper way up in the tree, is propagated largely by Hollywood. Snipers like to stay close to the ground. It gives you more options. If you do have to get up in a building with this equipment that is available today, and would have been available then, I would avoid something like that myself, but that's just me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So it's, in fact, an idea that laypeople have, people not specialised in sniping. We believe that you have to be high up somewhere to be able to shoot properly. Is that a false impression that we have?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: You can shoot properly from up high, but you stand the chance of isolating yourself. There have been a number of unfortunate incidents in my country of men shooting from buildings. Those men generally wind up dead because they can't get out of them before the police arrive. It's much the same in a military environment. One always leaves himself a way out. If you are in a tall building like that, shooting out the top of it, and eventually you're going to have to leave when people try to counter you, you're going to have to go through all those cold floors where somebody with a thermo-sight can spot you and ruin your day. That's just me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you right, if somebody is waiting for you downstairs, your friends, then there's no particular danger.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: You've got to get to them. Again, it's just -- it's just me. To say that -- that somebody not 100 per cent properly trained would do it, that's on them. I'm only giving my opinion here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will keep that photograph. Can we have an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D79, Your Honour -- I'm sorry, Exhibit D80.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: If you remember, a moment ago you discussed a particular incident with the Prosecution, an incident which took place on the 18th of November, 1994. We've just shown the location.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to have displayed on the screen, first of all, a report that we reviewed this morning as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is 65 ter 1484 admitted as Exhibit D19.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that exhibit, Mr. Jordan, do you remember that you said that several of your colleagues were there that day?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe I could reed your statement. This is paragraph 12. [In English] "Trevor Gibson from Scotland, Randy Henderson and Mark Anderson from the USA ..." [Interpretation] Were these people on site?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: I believed Todd Bayly was also there and I don't see his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is here. The first one to be mentioned, Todd Bayly from Montreal, if this is the same person we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: The document I'm talking at --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. Look at your own statement. Paragraph 12. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Pardon me, ma'am. I was looking at the monitor. I'm at paragraph 12, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, somewhere in the middle, Todd Bayly, Trevor Gibson, Randy Henderson and Mark Anderson are mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: These were the only members of your NGO, as far as you can remember, who were there at the time.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, they were the four men on duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Did the information you receive on that particular incident come from them as well?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes. I had spoke to all of them about the incident and they all gave me their versions, which varied slightly. But, yes, I spoke to them all about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Did these men agree on the specific location of the incident?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: The location of the incident was consistent with all the men. Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Is that the place that you've just encircled, put a circle around, on the photograph that we were looking at a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, the one I identified with a number 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Is that the place you saw on the photograph which was shown to you by the Prosecutor, where the poor kid can be seen on the ground?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me to say that this was on a zebra crossing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: I believe in the photo it shows the child down right on the white crossing marks. Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: As far as you can remember about this incident and the memories you have of other incidents, do you remember the relationship you had with the local police?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: I would have to say: Which local police? It was a bit of a joke with us that you never knew which local police you were going to be dealing with. The BiH forces did not have consistent command and control. I could have a pass saying that I could operate at night all over from one guy and go to respond to a fire at night and I would get stopped by somebody else's police. The police were inconsistent. You -- you know, they were like a box of chocolates; you never knew what you were going to get from them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jordan, normally when incidents took place -- we've heard here a lot of policemen who came to testify before this Chamber and they brought with them the reports that they'd established on the occasion of such incidents. Do you remember a specific incident which you witnessed -- first of all, do you remember any incident during which you personally were there at the time when the police came?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Some form of police would just about always show up. But as far as a police officer taking statements, pulling out a clipboard and doing a job like a police officer would do somewhere else, I literally cannot remember that happening. The only times I remember anything like that happening was when they were trying to give us a hard time about something, you know, a person -- we took a person's body out of a fire and took it to the morgue and dropped it off, and the next day they were at the fire station alleging some kind of incompetence on our part, you know, wanting details, and I basically told them to go to hell; you should have shown up at the fire. The police were, in my mind, nothing less than unprofessional. So no, I never saw them do anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Jordan. We'll deal with what we have. We have a report, among others, a report that is now being displayed on the screen. There is a translation in English as well. I would like us to focus on page 5 first, page 5 of this report that we have. Mr. Cerimagic Salko and Pilav Sulejman, the two drafters of this official report, and they're talking here about Mr. Joshua Wooding with UNHCR accreditation, a member of the GOFRS NGO, G-O-F-R-S. This is your colleague, Joshua?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: He was one of my personnel, yes. Josh.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So how do you explain the fact that they found Joshua and that Joshua didn't say anything about this incident to you, if I understood correctly?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Well, Josh probably did at one point or another. I just didn't -- it's 11 years. And as far as police reports go, a lot of these reports were generated after incidents that some of these cops weren't even at. I guess the best example is the Bosnian fire chief himself attended a function in Prague in 1995 and made a point of saying the west had completely abandoned the Sarajevo fire department, which I found a little bit miffing after three years of being involved and trying to do things. They developed reports to suit their agendas, not reflect the facts, in my regard.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe we should leave that document aside, but let me continue nevertheless. It is very interesting. Maybe it does confirm what you just said in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have a look at the English text because it's easier to read. In the B/C/S version, this is the page that is currently on the screen, and the corresponding paragraph is on the next page in the English version. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see the paragraph starting with "There was ..."?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Can you read it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes. Would you like me to read it out loud?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: "There was a blood-stain on the spot where the woman and the boy were wounded which members of UNPROFOR, who later arrived at the site, washed with water and later covered with earth, before the arrival of the on-site investigation team. The interview conducted at Sarajevo KCU admissions and triage dispensary yielded information --"

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: That will do, thank you. About that particular paragraph, it is quite unbelievable, isn't it, for people coming from normal countries, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to object. I don't think there is a foundation for this witness to start commenting on whether a report like this or what's recounted in the report is unbelievable or not. The witness was not at this event and the witness was not involved in law enforcement activities. He was involved in fire rescue activities. For him to comment on law enforcement procedures is really beyond his capacity. And so I think it's a question that is -- it goes way beyond his capacity and is irrelevant for that reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll allow the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, I'm not surprised that UNPROFOR personnel did that. There was an incident where we responded to an accident involving UN personnel whose tire had been shot out, and there was a car that went out of control and one man was killed and one was injured. We noted bullet-holes in the tire rim at the time of the accident, and when we went to look at the car the next day, the wheel was gone. So for whatever its own reasons, UNPROFOR -- you know, what doesn't happen they don't have to react to. They did that on occasion. I can't say they didn't because we just saw them do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this line of questioning was started by the Prosecutor on that specific incident, so I'd like to continue on, on that particular incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You know that on the spot a photograph was taken of this poor kid.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Are you referring, ma'am, to the Associated Press photo?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is the photograph showing the kid as well as two of your men --

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: -- on site where the incident took place.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, I have seen the photo.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe we could see this picture and discuss it for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is P272, 65 ter 2960.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: From what I understood - I have it here on paper, while we're waiting for it to be displayed on screen - this photograph was published the next day, the day after the incident took place, in the Providence Journal. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: If you saw so, ma'am. I didn't see it in the Providence Journal, but it could have happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please have a look at the upper part of -- maybe we could enlarge the picture a little.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: I see it, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Is this the Rhode Island Journal, this place where you come from?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Providence is the capital, and because our organisation originated in Rhode Island, a lot of our activities were quickly passed on to Rhode Island for local consumption. So I'm not surprised.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Do you, by any chance, remember how this picture was sent to the newspaper?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: No idea, ma'am, how these things occurred. But the media being the media, it wasn't my end.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: According to you, nobody from your NGO got in touch with a journalist from the Providence Journal.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: As far as I know, no. I'd have a problem with them if they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: This picture confirms what you said earlier, i.e., that the location where the incident took place is indeed the zebra crossing. This is shown on the picture; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: As far as you remember and according to the conversations you had with your colleagues, did anyone move the body of this poor kid at one stage or another, except, of course, when it was put into the van and brought to the morgue?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: It is my understanding that the child fell where he was hit and was not moved again until the guys put him in the ambulance after realising he was dead. It was a through-and-through gun-shot wound to the head, so there wasn't much question of that. As far as I understand, he fell where he was hit.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And, indeed, one of your colleagues saw him, talked to him a moment before, and saw him falling to the ground.

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes. The child had stopped by the fire truck and had talked to our guys. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jordan, in your answer to the Prosecutor's question, let me ask the question again: The building in the background, is it the museum building?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Is this the same building as the one we saw on the other photograph, the one you put some markings on?

utterances.speaker: JOHN JORDAN
utterances.text: I think I marked the museum, yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, I'm going to dismiss the witness for today. There's a matter I want to raise in private session. So, Mr. Jordan, you may leave now and return tomorrow at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 22nd day of February, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
